incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the victim of an artificial intelligence fraud scheme targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos depicting Leal offering immigration services he never provided, including false claims about obtaining US residency for $2,200. The scams escalated dramatically in recent months after potential clients began calling his office. Leal's anti-piracy company has removed nearly 6,500 fraudulent profiles across multiple platforms, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram.

The scammers typically use social media videos to direct victims to contact a phone number through WhatsApp, where they send fake contracts and request payment through apps like Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App. Other fraudulent videos feature fake testimonials from supposed clients praising Leal's services. Leal has warned immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to be cautious of immediate payment requests. He plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the fraud's origin.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fabricated article circulated online featuring a fake interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The fake story, which never actually occurred, depicted Bullock storming out over Kohler's questions. This incident exemplifies a growing category of scams using artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes of celebrities and politicians. ASIC reports that such schemes are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent.

ASIC's latest research reveals that investment scams jumped significantly, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams surged 279 percent, while fake investment platforms rose 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of impersonated public figures, followed by other politicians and financial experts. Scammers create elaborate deception networks combining fake news articles, websites, and advertisements to lure victims. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers independently and remain skeptical of investment opportunities promoted by famous faces.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
Oura, a smart ring company valued at $11 billion, faces a class action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco. The suit alleges that Oura falsely advertised the accuracy of its sleep tracking technology. The company markets rings priced at $300 and up, claiming they can track sleep stages with 95% accuracy comparable to hospital sleep labs. However, the lawsuit contends that Oura's sensors and algorithms cannot accurately detect the physiological signals needed to measure different sleep stages and instead rely on unreliable AI estimates no better than random guessing.

Oura disputed the allegations, stating it stands behind its scientific evidence and that multiple peer-reviewed studies validate its sleep staging accuracy. The company noted that while its rings estimate sleep stages using heart rate, movement, and temperature data, they are not medical devices and should not replace clinical sleep studies. It remains unclear whether ring owners can join the lawsuit or what compensation might result. This is not Oura's first legal challenge, as the company also faces an ongoing class action over allegedly collecting personal information without customer consent.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Security researchers at Gambit Security discovered that the Aurora ransomware group has been actively targeting ESXi servers since April 2026. The group developed a Linux variant of their ransomware that can encrypt virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. Researchers also found that Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks across ten organizations between April and May 2026. The agent was tasked with various hacking activities including network scanning, privilege enumeration, and credential attacks, though many attempts failed initially.

Additionally, researchers identified a second cluster of Aurora activity affecting eight organizations across multiple countries. This second group used different tactics, including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. The investigation revealed multiple command and control servers, SOCKS proxies, and the group's data leak website at exposedrecords.io. Researchers published technical indicators including IP addresses, file hashes, and domains associated with both Aurora clusters to help organizations identify and defend against these attacks.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A major Pizza Hut franchisee filed a lawsuit in Texas claiming the chain's new AI-powered delivery system called Dragontail caused over $100 million in damages. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut locations across the Northeast, alleges the system created operational problems after it gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen workflows. The franchisee says drivers began waiting to batch multiple orders together, sometimes delaying deliveries by up to fifteen minutes, and could see tip amounts, leading some to reject certain orders. Before the 2024 rollout, Chaac achieved over 90% on-time deliveries and double-digit sales growth, but afterward experienced sharp declines, including a swing from positive 10.19% to negative 9.78% year-over-year sales in New York City.

Chaac claims Pizza Hut failed to provide adequate training and support while mandating continued use of the problematic software, breaching their franchise agreement. The company is seeking more than $100 million in damages plus legal fees and other relief. Pizza Hut stated it is reviewing the claims and will respond through legal channels. This lawsuit comes as Pizza Hut faces broader struggles within its parent company Yum! Brands, which previously announced plans to close 250 US locations this year.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other "Fresh Air" staff members to defraud authors, entertainers, and public figures. The fraudulent emails appear highly personalized, reference the target's work, and propose interview opportunities. Victims eventually receive requests for payment, typically around $250 for alleged production costs. Historian Jennifer Black from Misericordia University received such an email and initially felt flattered before becoming suspicious when asked to pay. WHYY, NPR, and law enforcement are investigating the scheme, which has also targeted other celebrities including comedians Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler.

According to cybersecurity expert Aunshul Rege, artificial intelligence has made these social engineering scams more convincing and affordable to execute. Red flags include emails from unofficial addresses like terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com, requests for payment, and hosts personally handling logistics rather than using production assistants. WHYY has clarified it never charges guests for interviews. Experts recommend verifying requests through legitimate organization contacts and remaining skeptical of unsolicited interview offers, as AI-enabled scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated and personalized to specific targets.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
Israeli government officials and contractors created a fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute to produce propaganda content designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. Between August 6 and 14, the site published 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words, framing pro-Israel arguments on controversial topics like genocide allegations and Palestinian displacement. The reports were presented as academic research but persistently minimized criticism of Israel by claiming no court had ruled on genocide or apartheid claims. A commercial platform called Res was used to optimize the content so AI systems would cite it.

The operation is part of a larger campaign financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government, routed through the advertising company Havas Media and contractors including former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale's Clock Tower X. Israeli officials have expressed frustration that public diplomacy spending has failed to improve Israel's standing in American public opinion, which has declined significantly since 2022. Researchers warn that using AI systems to spread narratives makes fact-checking difficult, as chatbots may repeat claims without citing sources or acknowledging the material's origin.

Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno, alleging the companies scraped thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their systems. The labels claim both companies deliberately concealed their training data and that the services directly reproduce sections of famous songs. The lawsuits reference massive catalogs including works by The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Michael Jackson, and Mariah Carey, among many others.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate famous songs by using specific prompts describing musical characteristics like genre, era, and artist style. Examples include generating songs that closely mimicked Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and Green Day's "American Idiot," sometimes reproducing entire lyrics and melodies. The companies have been sued in New York and Massachusetts, and the labels submitted a thumb drive of AI-generated music as evidence. Both Udio and Suno previously claimed their training practices constitute fair use.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers in a Los Angeles lawsuit have admitted to using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases and citations in their court filings. The homeowner's attorney discovered that the motions contained nonexistent cases, fabricated quotes, and false legal holdings. The lawsuit involves Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, whose Carson home was damaged by fire in 2020, and later suffered water damage during repairs. After State Farm allegedly delayed approving repairs, the reconstruction was never completed, leaving Meni-Siliga and her husband bankrupt and homeless after draining their savings and retirement accounts. State Farm named them, the contractor, and a public adjuster as defendants in their original answer to the complaint.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys to help prepare filings, mistakenly believing it was connected to her law firm's Westlaw subscription and would verify citations. She confirmed that seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fake quotes. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized to the court and accepted responsibility for the filings. The trial is scheduled for October. AI hallucinations in legal work are becoming increasingly common, with 41 percent of law firms now using generative AI, and a database tracking 1,922 documented cases of legal hallucinations worldwide.

stories.Headline: China promotes coordinated development of data industry, artificial intelligence-- Beijing Review
stories.Summary:
# Summary

China's data industry reached 6.78 trillion yuan in 2025, and the country is now focusing on coordinating development between its data sector and artificial intelligence capabilities. The 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo, held in Guiyang from August 28-30, attracted 372 companies and over 16,000 guests to showcase innovations in computing power, large models, and data circulation. Government officials emphasized that high-quality datasets are essential for advancing AI capabilities and that data technology is transforming traditional industries like power generation and renewable energy forecasting.

Beyond upgrading existing industries, data and AI are creating new business opportunities and employment categories. Companies are hiring data collectors to train robots through embodied intelligence projects, while micro-enterprises and one-person startups are emerging as signs of entrepreneurial growth. International participants from Zimbabwe, Chile, Pakistan, and other nations attended to explore cooperation opportunities, with officials highlighting the potential for shared benefits and technological exchange between countries through collaborative data and AI development.

stories.Headline: Who Writes AI's Rules When Someone Else Owns the Machines?
stories.Summary:
# Summary

South Africa withdrew its Draft National AI Policy in April 2026 after discovering that at least six of its 67 academic references were fabricated, highlighting a broader challenge facing the Global South. The incident underscores a critical debate about who controls artificial intelligence governance and infrastructure. Currently, the United States and China host roughly 86% of global data centre capacity, giving them power to set rules and prices for AI systems worldwide. This concentration of computing power represents what critics call "tech colonialism," where developing nations provide data and demand but lack ownership and control over the technology itself.

BRICS countries and other Global South nations are attempting to shift AI governance away from Western-led standards by emphasizing digital sovereignty and development rights. They are seeking to anchor AI governance within the United Nations rather than OECD-led bodies and have established organizations like the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. However, meaningful sovereignty requires owning physical infrastructure, not just adopting policies. The article notes that until developing nations build regional computing capacity and chip manufacturing capabilities, they remain dependent on foreign platforms controlled by American hyperscalers or Chinese firms. True sovereignty means choosing dependencies rather than having them imposed.

stories.Headline: CSA's Top Cloud Threats: Identity, AI -- Campus Technology
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Security Alliance surveyed 507 security professionals to identify the top threats to cloud computing in 2026. Identity and access management issues rose to the number one concern, moving up from second place in 2024, while misconfiguration dropped to fifth. Two artificial intelligence-related threats appeared in the rankings for the first time, including AI-enhanced attacks and AI system compromise. The top eleven threats also include insecure third-party resources, insecure APIs, advanced persistent threats, and inadequate cloud security strategy and governance.

The survey results reveal a significant shift in the cloud threat landscape, with organizations now prioritizing identity protection, artificial intelligence risks, and software supply chains over infrastructure-focused concerns. Security scores ranged closely from 7.95 for identity and access management to 7.45 for system vulnerabilities. The report aims to help organizations make informed risk-management decisions about cloud adoption by providing expert analysis of technical and business impacts, real-world examples, and corresponding security controls across cloud and AI environments.

stories.Headline: EU places ChatGPT, Reddit, Roblox under strictest platform rules
stories.Summary:
The European Union has classified ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine and designated Reddit and Roblox as Very Large Online Platforms under its Digital Services Act. These three American companies will now face direct supervision from the European Commission and must comply with stricter requirements designed to address risks related to children, election integrity, and public security. The rules apply to services with over 45 million users in the EU, bringing the total number of regulated platforms to 28.

Companies failing to meet the new requirements within four months face fines up to 6 percent of their annual global revenue. Reddit reported 57.2 million EU users in July, while Roblox has 46.6 million. OpenAI stated it would prepare to meet ChatGPT's additional obligations, and Roblox welcomed the designation, emphasizing safety's importance. This designation adds another regulatory layer for ChatGPT, which already complies with the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act.

The administration launched the AI Talent Ark Project this year to nurture talent through fundamental education, professional development, and data-driven approaches, aiming to build a large AI talent pool and strengthen Taiwan's competitiveness in technology sectors.

The government is also prioritizing technological sovereignty and national resilience. The Minister of Digital Affairs announced plans to accumulate at least 10,000 graphics processing units through private investment in AI computing centers within a year. Taiwan is focusing on developing sovereign AI systems that understand Taiwanese perspectives and languages, along with low-Earth-orbit satellite communications to ensure independent communication capabilities. Officials emphasized that technological sovereignty means focusing on critical technologies rather than developing every technology domestically.

stories.Headline: Hock Tan Guided Broadcom Past $100 Billion of AI Revenue in 2027. The Stock Is 25% off Its High.
stories.Summary:
Broadcom CEO Hock Tan has predicted the company will generate over $100 billion in artificial intelligence semiconductor revenue by fiscal 2027, a projection he reiterated during the company's June earnings call. The company demonstrated strong progress toward this goal, reporting $10.8 billion in AI semiconductor revenue in the fiscal second quarter of 2026, representing a 143% increase year over year, with expectations for $16 billion in the third quarter. Tan's forecast is backed by specific customer commitments including long-term agreements with Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta Platforms, plus $6 billion in purchase orders from two additional customers.

Despite this growth trajectory, Broadcom's stock has declined significantly, currently trading around $370, which is approximately 25% below its 52-week high of $495. The stock's weakness reflects investor concerns about three factors: timing, since the revenue is weighted toward the back half of fiscal 2027, customer concentration among six major clients, and execution risk. The company's upcoming September 2 earnings report will provide important checkpoints showing whether the company maintains its full-year $56 billion AI revenue guidance and its longer-term $100 billion forecast.

Taiwan Semiconductor benefits from a neutral position in the competition between chip designers, meaning it will profit regardless of which company's hardware becomes dominant. To support this strategy, OptiValue has formed partnerships with Eagle Infrastructure India for intelligent infrastructure development and with SFJ Business Solutions for AI transformation programmes. Chairman Ashish Kumar emphasized the company's goal to connect artificial intelligence with physical systems across defence and critical infrastructure, positioning digital twins as a bridge between digital engineering and operational intelligence for improved organizational resilience.
